displayQuote: The world breaks everyone, and afterward many are strong at the broken places

meta.title: Who really said "The world breaks everyone, and afterward many are strong at the broken places"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuine Hemingway. It is Chapter XXXIV of A Farewell to Arms (1929) — though the 1929 text reads “every one,” and the next sentence is far darker.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The world breaks everyone, and afterward many are strong at the broken places'?
meta.ogDescription: Really Hemingway: A Farewell to Arms, Chapter XXXIV, 1929. But the original prints “every one,” and the quote is almost always cut one sentence too early.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Genuine, and easy to pin down: the sentence is narrator Frederic Henry’s interior monologue in Chapter XXXIV of A Farewell to Arms, first published by Charles Scribner’s Sons in September 1929. The 1929 text prints it as “The world breaks every one and afterward many are strong at the broken places” — two words, no comma.

source.heading: Where the line actually appears

docMeta.dd: New York: Charles Scribner’s Sons, September 1929 (serialised in Scribner’s Magazine, May–October 1929)
Frederic Henry, the novel’s first-person narrator

source.excerpt: If people bring so much courage to this world the world has to kill them to break them, so of course it kills them. The world breaks every one and afterward many are strong at the broken places. But those that will not break it kills. It kills the very good and the very gentle and the very brave impartially. If you are none of these you can be sure it will kill you too but there will be no special hurry.
trail: The sentence appears verbatim in Chapter XXXIV of the Project Gutenberg full text ↗ of A Farewell to Arms, transcribed from the 1929 Charles Scribner’s Sons edition, where it reads “The world breaks every one and afterward many are strong at the broken places.”
Wikiquote ↗ lists the line in its sourced section under A Farewell to Arms (1929), Chapter 34 — not among the disputed or misattributed entries.

Quote Investigator ↗ treats the 1929 passage as authentic Hemingway while debunking the separate, blended saying “We are all broken. That’s how the light gets in,” which it says was “not crafted by Ernest Hemingway.”
Publication history ↗: serialised in Scribner’s Magazine from the May to October 1929 issues and published as a book in September 1929, with a first print run of about 31,000 copies.

author.name: Ernest Hemingway
author.heading: Who was Ernest Hemingway?
author.metaLine: 1899–1961 · American novelist, short-story writer & war correspondent
author.bio: Ernest Hemingway was born in Oak Park, Illinois on 21 July 1899 and died on 2 July 1961. He drove an ambulance on the Italian front in the First World War, the experience he rebuilt as fiction in A Farewell to Arms (1929). He won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 1953 and the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1954 — and, thanks to a prose style that is easy to imitate badly, he is now one of the most misquoted writers on the internet.

misattribution.heading: What gets changed, and what gets falsely added
misattribution.intro: The attribution is right — this one really is Hemingway. What goes wrong is the wording, the stopping point, and a neighbouring saying that borrows his authority.

items.why: The Scribner’s text of 1929 prints every one as two words: “The world breaks every one and afterward many are strong at the broken places.” You can read the sentence in place in Chapter XXXIV of the Project Gutenberg full text ↗. The one-word spelling is a modernisation, not Hemingway’s.

items.who: “some are strong at the broken places”
items.why: A widely copied aggregator version swaps many for some and adds commas — BrainyQuote ↗ carries it as “The world breaks everyone, and afterward, some are strong at the broken places.” The 1929 text says many.

items.who: “We are all broken. That’s how the light gets in.”
items.why: Constantly pinned on Hemingway, and constantly confused with this line. Quote Investigator ↗ concludes it “was not crafted by Ernest Hemingway,” hypothesising instead that his 1929 sentence and Leonard Cohen’s 1992 lyric about cracks and light both shaped it; the Hemingway ascription entered circulation by 2013.

The sentence is not an authorial motto: it sits inside the first-person narration of Lieutenant Frederic Henry, and in the printed paragraph ↗ it is immediately followed by “But those that will not break it kills.” The uplift is real; so is the sentence that cancels it.

misattribution.truthLine: The line is authentically Hemingway’s — A Farewell to Arms, Chapter XXXIV, published by Charles Scribner’s Sons in 1929 and now free to read in full ↗. Quote it as he wrote it, and ideally do not stop at the full stop.

context.heading: Why the sentence keeps getting cut in half
lead: Chapter XXXIV is the calm in the middle of the storm. Frederic Henry has deserted the Italian army, found Catherine again, and for a few pages the novel simply lets him be happy — which is exactly when Hemingway drops the coldest paragraph in the book. The consoling clause everyone posts is the second sentence of five, and the three that follow it take the comfort straight back: “But those that will not break it kills. It kills the very good and the very gentle and the very brave impartially.”

Quoted whole, it is a shrug at an indifferent universe. Quoted from the full stop after “broken places,” it becomes a greetings-card promise that suffering makes you stronger. Both versions are Hemingway’s words; only one is his point.
detailsBody: The novel reached readers twice in 1929: serialised in Scribner’s Magazine across the May to October issues, then published in book form by Charles Scribner’s Sons in September, with a first print run of roughly 31,000 copies.

The passage is written in the first person by Lieutenant Frederic Henry, the novel’s narrator — not delivered as an authorial aphorism. That distinction is usually lost the moment the sentence is lifted out of the paragraph.
context.pull: The line everyone shares stops one full stop before the line that undoes it.
